source: Wang et al. (2023) PopBlends: Strategies for Conceptual Blending with Large Language Models (CHI '23)
finding: PopBlends splits blending into two stages: find a connecting concept between a pop-culture domain and a product, then find scenes for it. Three ways to find connecting concepts were compared: No-GPT (plot matching), Half-GPT (GPT-3 attributes of entities), Full-GPT (GPT-3 lists concepts directly). All three worked about equally well.
numbers: Annotators judged connecting concepts. Success (related to both domains): No-GPT 56.0%, Half-GPT 55.3%, Full-GPT 58.7%; overall 56.7%. At least one good concept in the top 5: 90.0%, 96.6%, 93.3%; overall 93.3% of pop-culture/product pairs.
limits: GPT-3 (2021 model). A concept counted as good only if both the pop-culture and the product question were marked true; if two raters disagreed, one 'true' was enough. Only 5 pop-culture domains and 6 products.
agent_relevance: Per-item accuracy of an LLM blend proposer is only about 55 to 60%, but 5 proposals give a good one about 93% of the time. Over-generate, then let a checker or a person filter: fits O7 with a selection step.

source: Wang et al. (2023) PopBlends: Strategies for Conceptual Blending with Large Language Models (CHI '23)
finding: Accuracy of GPT-3 generated entity attributes (used for the Half-GPT stage) depends on attribute type. Made-up catchphrases and activities were weakest.
numbers: 10 annotators. Mean 2.86 of 5 (57%) overall, inter-rater reliability 0.41. Adjectives 3.93 (79%, IRR 0.47), activities 2.89 (58%, IRR 0.32), catchphrases 1.75 (35%, IRR 0.41). Attribute-to-product similarity scores as low as 0.16-0.17 got through when no cut-off was used.
limits: Moderate rater agreement. Authors note GPT-3 sometimes invents connections for obscure entities.
agent_relevance: Free-text blend inputs contain confabulated attributes. A similarity cut-off or a grounding check on each input-space element is needed before mapping (supports an input check in S3).

source: Wang et al. (2023) PopBlends: Strategies for Conceptual Blending with Large Language Models (CHI '23)
finding: Stage 2 (scenes for a connecting concept) was more accurate for product scenes than for pop-culture plot scenes.
numbers: Scene related to the connecting concept: product scenes 89.1% vs pop-culture scenes 75.9% (13.2 points lower). At least one of two scenes related: 98.3% for product scenes, 92.3% on average when the connecting words were good.
limits: Figures from the system paper; correctness judged by annotators, not creative value.
agent_relevance: Elaboration of a blend is reliable when it draws on well-covered general knowledge and weak when it draws on a narrow world. Pick the richer space as the base for run-the-blend steps.

source: Wang et al. (2023) PopBlends: Strategies for Conceptual Blending with Large Language Models (CHI '23)
finding: Within-subjects user study: PopBlends users produced more blend ideas than users with internet search, with less workload.
numbers: N=10. Ideas per pop-culture/product pair: 2.03 (SD 0.84) with PopBlends vs 0.87 (SD 0.56) baseline, paired Wilcoxon p<0.001. NASA-TLX, Bonferroni corrected: mental demand 2.85 vs 5.80 (p=0.004), performance 2.10 vs 3.60 (p=0.004), effort 3.05 vs 5.00 (p=0.006), frustration 1.65 vs 3.25 (p=0.026), temporal demand 3.00 vs 4.65 (p=0.028); physical demand not significant (p=0.102). All 10 said PopBlends helped more.
limits: N=10 amateur designers, 6 pairs each. Counts of ideas, not quality ratings. Baseline was web search, not a plain LLM chat.
agent_relevance: The gain came from recognition over recall: show candidate bridges and let the person pick. For our agent, a list of candidate bridging concepts beats a blank 'blend these two' prompt. Not tested against a plain LLM prompt.

source: Ge and Parikh (2021) Visual Conceptual Blending with Large-scale Language and Vision Models
finding: Used masked-language-model prompts as a two-step blend: 'the moon is like a [MASK]' gives a related object, then 'the ghost has the property of [MASK]' gives the hinge property, then a template sentence. A second shape-guided prompt gave visually similar objects (moon -> shell, egg, fruit).
numbers: Property-prediction test on 66,442 property-object pairs from a simile dataset, 1000 candidates per method. Precision at top 1000: ConceptNet 5.90 vs best language model 66.38. Values for the middle rows (ELMo, BERT-base, BERT-large, GPT) run 37.33 to 66.38 but the table is garbled in the text layer. P@10 for all methods only 0.13 to 2.59.
limits: Table extraction garbled. Masked-LM era (BERT, ELMo, GPT-1), not instruction-tuned LLMs. Property recovery is a proxy, not blend quality.
agent_relevance: Early evidence that a language model fills the shared-property slot (generic space) better than a knowledge base. In our agent 'what property do the inputs share' can be its own explicit step.

source: Ge and Parikh (2021) Visual Conceptual Blending with Large-scale Language and Vision Models
finding: Human preference study on 20 blend descriptions (10 machine-written, 10 by the authors) rendered with BigSleep, DeepDaze and DF-GAN. Large language-image models beat the GAN baseline; BigSleep was preferred over DeepDaze.
numbers: 20 descriptions rated on Amazon Mechanical Turk; differences marked significant at 95% confidence in the paper's Figure 3 (exact preference percentages not in the text layer).
limits: Small stimulus set, old image models. Reports preference only, no creativity score.
agent_relevance: Pipeline pattern: language model reasons, a separate generator renders. Rendering the blend was the quality bottleneck, not choosing the concept.

source: Sato (2025) The Way We Prompt: Conceptual Blending, Neural Dynamics, and Prompt-Induced Transitions in LLMs
finding: Single-author review that maps Fauconnier-Turner onto prompting: prompt elements are input spaces, pretraining knowledge is the generic space, generated text is the blend. Names two phenomena: Prompt-Induced Transition (tone or meaning shift, e.g. aperiodic tiling plus craft) and Prompt-Induced Hallucination (plausible but ungrounded output from blending distant domains, e.g. periodic table plus tarot).
numbers: No measurements, no sample sizes, no statistics. Case examples only.
limits: Essay with anecdotes from the author's own prompting. No replication. Neural parallels are speculative.
agent_relevance: A warning: blending far-apart domains can give fluent but ungrounded output. The elaboration step needs a grounding check. Weak evidence; treat as hypothesis.

source: Radensky et al. (2026) Scideator: Human-LLM Compound System for Scientific Ideation through Facet Recombination and Novelty Evaluation (CAIS '26)
finding: An LLM loop that extracts facets (purpose, mechanism, evaluation) from papers, recombines facets across analogous papers into ideas, then checks novelty against retrieved literature and suggests a facet swap if the idea is not novel. This is blend-style recombination inside a loop.
numbers: Within-subjects user study N=22 computer scientists. Creativity Support Index median 70.50 (Q1 57.50, Q3 79.00) vs 61.00 (Q1 42.25, Q3 71.50) for a same-LLM baseline; Wilcoxon V=208.5, p<.01. Rated newness of the favourite idea only slightly higher (median difference 0.5 on 7 points). 14 participants noted gains in expressiveness.
limits: Self-reported creativity support, not expert-judged novelty of final ideas. Newness advantage small. CS researchers only. The authors' own system.
agent_relevance: Closest published match to our need: generate by recombining structured parts, then run a separate novelty check that feeds back as a repair move. Gains came mostly from exploration breadth, not rated newness.

source: Radensky et al. (2026) Scideator
finding: Ablations: structuring ideas into facets helps the novelty checker too. Facet-based retrieve-then-rerank surfaced more relevant papers than standard retrieval, and a facet-grounded novelty classifier beat classifiers that reason over unstructured text.
numbers: Direction taken from the abstract; exact ablation scores not extracted in this session.
limits: Directional claim only; check the paper tables before using numbers.
agent_relevance: Structured inputs (named slots) make later checking more reliable than free text. Supports keeping blend inputs as slotted structures.

source: Matsuhira et al. (2024) Investigating Conceptual Blending of a Diffusion Model for Improving Nonword-to-Image Generation (ACM MM '24)
finding: Stable Diffusion depicts blended concepts without training for it when the text embedding is an interpolation between two concept embeddings. The effect is strongest at the midpoint and falls off near either end.
numbers: 1,000 images over 9 interpolation ratios. At the midpoint, Blended Concept Depiction (narrow sense) 0.621 and Mixed Concept Depiction (broad) 0.862. Averaged over all ratios 0.389 and 0.471. Concept A depiction rises from 0.152 to 1.000 and concept B falls from 1.000 to 0.265 across ratios.
limits: Image model; single-concept classifiers decide what is depicted. Authors attribute blending mainly to specific dimensions of the text embedding space; mechanism not settled.
agent_relevance: Blending has a sweet spot in the middle of the mix; extreme weights give just one input. For prompting, give both inputs equal salience.

source: Matsuhira et al. (2024) Nonword-to-Image
finding: Their proposed embedding conversion (k-nearest-neighbour search plus linear regression) improved image quality over the usual MLP converter and is expected to keep blending at a similar rate to ground-truth embeddings.
numbers: Ground-truth embeddings give blended depiction in up to 60% of images (midpoint).
limits: Image domain; evaluation uses classifier proxies.
agent_relevance: Blend occurrence can be measured as a rate. Our agent could estimate how often its blends really contain both inputs.

source: Olearo et al. (2024) How to Blend Concepts in Diffusion Models
finding: Compared four ways to blend two text concepts in Stable Diffusion (text-embedding blend TEXTUAL, prompt switching SWITCH, alternating prompts ALTERNATE, a new U-Net conditioning method UNET). No single method was best; the best depends on the type of blend.
numbers: Survey of 23 participants (21 complete) ranking 4 methods on 24 concept pairs in 4 categories. Mean rank (lower is better), global: SWITCH 2.26, TEXTUAL 2.54, ALTERNATE 2.61, UNET 2.68. Animal pairs: TEXTUAL best 1.98. Object+animal: SWITCH best 2.15. Compound words: SWITCH best 2.31. Real-life scenarios: SWITCH best 2.13.
limits: Small panel, small stimulus set, small overall rank gaps, Stable Diffusion 1.x era.
agent_relevance: The combination operator should match the kind of inputs; one fixed recipe is not enough. Argues for a menu of blend strategies chosen per case.

source: Cho et al. (2025) Imagine for Me: Creative Conceptual Blending of Real Images and Text via Blended Attention (IT-Blender)
finding: An adapter for SD 1.5 and FLUX that blends a reference image concept with a text-named object. Motivated by human design fixation. Beats encoder-based and inversion-based baselines.
numbers: DINO similarity between generated and reference image: IT-Blender 0.837 vs IP-Adapter 0.812 vs BLIP-Diffusion 0.821. ChatGPT-4.1 gave a blending score; FLUX test used 200 unseen samples x 20 text prompts (4,000 per baseline).
limits: Preprint, under review. LLM-judge blending score and DINO similarity are proxies for creative quality.
agent_relevance: Automating the combination step is meant to beat human anchoring on one input. An agent can do the same by forcing both inputs to be projected.

source: Cho et al. (2025) IT-Blender
finding: An LLM judge with a detailed rubric scored blends, and its comments for top 10%, median and bottom 90% samples name which input was dropped (e.g. 'only the visual reference style, no rabbit').
numbers: Comments quoted for ranked samples; no agreement with human raters reported in the part read.
limits: LLM-judge validity not tested against humans in the part read.
agent_relevance: A cheap check: ask a separate call whether both inputs are visible in the blend, and which one was dropped.

source: Cho et al. (2025) IT-Blender (reporting Sun et al. 2025, Creative Blends)
finding: As reported in Cho et al., a system that takes several textual concepts and outputs one blended image reduced cognitive load and fostered creativity in a user study.
numbers: No numbers in the citing paper; the original was not opened.
limits: Second-hand report.
agent_relevance: Supports 'visualise the blend to lower load'. For an agent: render the blend as a concrete scene or worked example before judging it.

source: Xu et al. (2026) Beyond Pixels: Visual Metaphor Transfer via Schema-Driven Agentic Reasoning
finding: A four-agent pipeline (perception, transfer, generation, diagnostic) that operationalises blending: extract a schema from a reference ad image (generic space = relational logic, carrier, violation points), re-instantiate it for a new subject, generate, then check and loop back.
numbers: Human study, 100 participants (age 14-55, 45 male). Mean ratings on 5 scales (MR, MI, VA, VI, VQ): full model 4.47, 4.56, 4.51, 4.74, 4.76; without diagnostic agent 4.26, 4.05, 3.98, 4.61, 4.48; without transfer agent 4.01, 3.71, 3.83, 4.33, 4.25. Further ablations (no CBT description, no schema vocabulary, no backtracking) also lowered quality; numbers in figure only.
limits: Authors' own ablation, preprint. Compared against Midjourney, GPT-Image, BAGEL, Banana-pro. Subjective ratings. Advertising metaphors only.
agent_relevance: Best direct evidence that explicit generic-space extraction plus a check-and-backtrack loop beats a single instruction. Largest drop came from removing the transfer step that picks a new carrier.

source: Xu et al. (2026) Beyond Pixels
finding: Baseline behaviour with a simple instruction ('understand this advertisement image, analyze its metaphors and transfer this creative idea to the new product') was to fall back to literal object substitution or the salient surface content. The model skips the generic-space step unless forced.
numbers: Qualitative observation, paired with the ablation numbers in the other record.
limits: Authors' description.
agent_relevance: Failure mode of unaided blending: copying one input's surface. A schema prompt with named slots (subject, carrier, generic meaning, violation) prevents it.

source: Misty: UI Prototyping Through Interactive Conceptual Blending (CHI '25)
finding: GPT-4o based tool that blends example UIs (screenshots, sketches) into a source UI by global blending, drag-and-drop, regenerate, or semantic diff. Users used imperfect blend outputs as springboards.
numbers: 14 frontend developers, mean 36.3 min with the tool (sd 7.0), 103 blending operations (mean 7.4 per person). Mix: global blending 36 (34.95%), drag-and-drop 35 (33.98%), regenerate 19 (18.5%), semantic diff 9 (8.74%), code edit 4 (3.88%). Satisfaction after each operation averaged 3.2 of 5 (sd 1.3).
limits: No control condition. Satisfaction only 3.2 of 5. Participants noted model limits on perfect blends.
agent_relevance: Real use split about evenly between whole-input blends and fine-grained selective projection. Mid satisfaction means a repair or edit step is needed.

source: Lynn (2026) Conceptual blending in humans and language models (Frontiers in Psychology)
finding: Conceptual analysis: human blends are 'generative-causal' (a goal selects affordances from the inputs); LLM blends are 'distributionally novel', with goals supplied from outside by prompt and alignment. A toy goal-driven blend is built as a vector symbolic architecture in Python.
numbers: No human or model experiment; one toy implementation. Published 29 July 2026.
quote: The goal is not merely an externally applied instruction; it is an active parent node within the generative hierarchy
limits: Theory paper. The claim that LLM goal-direction is only external is untested; the author concedes models may encode goal-like structure.
agent_relevance: The goal that decides which input features survive must be kept visible in the context. Matches keeping the goal explicit in S3.

source: Lynn (2026) Conceptual blending in humans and language models
finding: Notes the open debate on whether LLM concepts are grounded: some work says models acquire key features of conceptual competence, others say missing sensorimotor grounding sets limits.
numbers: No data. Cites Mollo and Millière 2026, Ma and Narayanan 2026, Xu et al. 2025 for the first view; Bender and Koller 2020, Pavlick 2023, Shanahan 2023 for the second.
limits: Position paper.
agent_relevance: Do not assume an LLM blend is physically consistent. A check against affordances or constraints is a separate step.

source: Keon et al. (2025) Galton's Law of Mediocrity: Why LLMs Regress to the Mean and Fail at Creativity in Advertising
finding: When ad ideas were simplified step by step and models asked to regenerate, creative features (metaphor, emotion, visual cues) vanished first while factual content stayed. Regeneration gave longer, lexically varied text that did not recover the original's distinctiveness. Giving creative cues helped partly.
numbers: Over 1,000 advertising ideas; metrics cosine similarity, METEOR, entropy, n-gram uniqueness, plus human and LLM judgement. Effect sizes not extracted this session.
limits: Advertising only; company-owned database. Not a blending test, but shows the failure a blend step faces: the non-obvious emergent part is lost.
agent_relevance: Unaided LLM output regresses to the typical. A blend step should carry explicit markers of the unusual projected element and test that it survived to the output.

source: Khojasteh et al. (2026) Enhancing Structural Mapping with LLM-derived Abstractions for Analogical Reasoning in Narratives (YARN)
finding: Pipeline for the cross-space mapping part: an LLM splits stories into units and abstracts each at four levels, then a structural-mapping module aligns them. Mapping on raw text embeddings fails; abstractions fix it.
numbers: Mapping without abstraction is below chance: Qwen 0.17 on StoryAnalogy-MCQ (chance 0.25) and 0.24 on ARN far analogy (chance 0.50). With conceptual plus evaluative abstraction: Qwen 0.46, Llama 0.45 on MCQ (Llama from 0.16, +0.29). Conceptual alone 0.41 for Qwen.
limits: Analogy in narratives, not blend output. Best results still under 0.5 on 4-way MCQ.
agent_relevance: Cross-space mapping needs roles abstracted first; surface similarity misleads. Supports a step that rewrites each input at the level of roles before mapping.

source: Eppe et al. (2018) A computational framework for conceptual blending (Artificial Intelligence)
finding: From the COINVENT project: input spaces as logical theories, generic space by generalising the inputs, blends found by search over consistent combinations with consistency checks by a theorem prover.
numbers: Not opened; no figures recorded.
limits: Known from the OpenAlex listing and prior knowledge only; read before using any claim.
agent_relevance: Oldest rigorous recipe for the generic-space step, plus a logic consistency check that could screen LLM blends.

source: Pereira (2006) Experiments with free concept generation in Divago
finding: Divago: knowledge base, mapper, blender, and a constraint-based factory searching for the best blend with a genetic algorithm.
numbers: Not opened (download failed); no numbers.
limits: Prior knowledge only; unverified detail.
agent_relevance: Generate-many-and-score by optimality constraints is the pre-LLM form of the loop; an LLM can now be the proposer and a scorer the constraints.

source: Chilton, Petridis, Agrawala (2019) VisiBlends: A Flexible Workflow for Visual Blends (CHI '19)
finding: Human-in-the-loop workflow: pick concepts, find associated symbols, find images with a shared shape, merge the aligned parts. Cited in opened papers as prior work.
numbers: Not opened; no numbers.
limits: Known only as cited by Ge and Parikh and by Cho et al.
agent_relevance: A shared shape or structure as the bridge is a repeated design choice: a concrete generic space.
